benchmark_name: MentalHospital: A Virtual Environment for Evaluating Psychiatric Clinical Encounters
authors: Yuming Yang; Xiao Sun; Yuanwei Zou; Zhengxiao Wu; Yun Chen; Jiang Zhong; Haoyang Zeng; Jingwang Huang; Kaiwen Wei
institutions: School of Computer Science, Chongqing University, Chongqing, China; School of Computer Science, Hunan University, Changsha, China
ground_truth_source: 1,193 de-identified psychiatric electronic health record (EHR) cases from six medical centers across three regions, independently reviewed by two licensed psychiatrists (Cohen's κ > 0.8)
size_of_benchmark: 1,193 psychiatric EHR cases (885 single-diagnosis, 308 comorbid); 76 disorder-level diagnoses across all major ICD-11 psychiatric categories
what_assessed_skills: Psychiatric clinical encounter competence: subjective interviewing (symptom/history elicitation), objective examination (auxiliary exam recommendation), diagnostic assessment (clinical note generation, category and disorder-level diagnosis), treatment planning; plus process-level skills: communication empathy, interviewing professionalism, clinical-note quality, diagnostic rigor, treatment appropriateness
tasks_assessed: Multi-turn psychiatric patient interview (subjective interviewing); auxiliary examination recommendation; clinical note generation; diagnostic category identification; disorder-level diagnosis ranking (nDCG); treatment plan generation
population_represented: Psychiatric patients across all major ICD-11 categories (76 disorders); multi-center records from six medical centers across three regions in China; age range ~5–75 years; both single-diagnosis and comorbid cases
num_domains: 4 (S.O.A.P. stages: Subjective Interviewing, Objective Examination, Diagnostic Assessment, Treatment Planning)
evaluation_method: Both (Automated + Human). Dual-track protocol: (1) Objective comparison — automated reference coverage matching against EHR-derived checkpoints using semantic similarity threshold τ=0.85 with Multi-LLM-assisted semantic matching; metrics include coverage %, category identification accuracy, disorder-level nDCG, examination F1/Jaccard. (2) Subjective assessment — MentalEval (five Qwen3-8B-based fine-tuned evaluators) scoring on 1–5 Likert scale for empathy, professionalism, note quality, diagnostic rigor, treatment appropriateness; MentalEval trained via rubric-grounded SFT + expert-guided DPO; validated against 22 clinician survey ratings and expert-rated test sets (QWK=0.944 average).
llms_evaluated: Llama-3-8B; Qwen3-14B; GPT-OSS-20B; QWQ-32B; GPT-OSS-120B; Claude-Sonnet-4.6; DeepSeek-V4-Pro; GPT-5.5; MedGemma-4B-it; MedGemma-27B-it; Baichuan-M2; (also human experts and medical trainees as baselines)
mental_health_conditions: All major ICD-11 psychiatric categories including: Schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders; Mood disorders (bipolar, depressive); Anxiety or fear-related disorders; Obsessive-compulsive or related disorders; Disorders specifically associated with stress (PTSD, adjustment disorder); Dissociative disorders; Personality disorders; Neurodevelopmental disorders; Neurocognitive disorders; Disorders due to substance use or addictive behaviors; Feeding or eating disorders; Bodily distress disorders; Catatonia; Elimination disorders; Disorders associated with pregnancy/childbirth; Disruptive behavior/dissocial disorders; 76 disorder-level diagnoses total
performance_scores: Best LLM (Baichuan-M2) objective scores: Inter. 51.29%, Exam. 24.76%, Note 50.54%, Cate. 80.56%, Diso. 43.19%; Human Experts: Inter. 82.35%, Exam. 91.90%, Note 88.67%, Cate. 90.59%, Diso. 83.24%; strongest LLM trails human experts by 37.28 percentage points average; GPT-5.5 highest on interviewing (69.06%) and category (70.23%); MentalEval average QWK=0.944 vs. LLM-as-a-Judge QWK=0.677
short_summary: MentalHospital is a virtual evaluation environment for assessing LLMs on complete psychiatric clinical encounters following the S.O.A.P. workflow (Subjective Interviewing, Objective Examination, Diagnostic Assessment, Treatment Planning). It is grounded in 1,193 de-identified psychiatric EHR cases from six Chinese medical centers, covering all major ICD-11 categories and 76 disorders, with skill-augmented standardized patient agents featuring dynamic memory recall. Each encounter is evaluated through a dual-track protocol combining automated objective comparison against EHR-derived references and subjective assessment via MentalEval, a suite of five Qwen3-8B-based domain-specific evaluators (covering empathy, professionalism, note quality, diagnostic rigor, treatment appropriateness) trained with rubric-grounded SFT and expert-guided DPO. Twelve LLMs were benchmarked alongside human experts and medical trainees; even the strongest LLM (Baichuan-M2) trails human experts by 37.28 percentage points in objective psychiatric competence, with mental status assessment identified as a key bottleneck. MentalEval achieves strong expert alignment (average QWK=0.944), and 22 clinicians rated MentalHospital's clinical fidelity at 3.88/5.

benchmark_name: Wavelet Scattering Transform for Interpretable Schizophrenia Biomarker Discovery and Classification from Resting-State EEG
authors: Md. Taksimul Ahsan Tawhid; Nasif Ahmed Rafe; Alif Tahmid Priyom; K. M. Mustafizur Rahman
institutions: Department of EECE, Military Institute of Science and Technology (MIST), Mirpur Cantonment, Dhaka, Bangladesh
ground_truth_source: Publicly available Kaggle dataset of adolescents screened by psychiatrist: 39 healthy controls and 45 with schizophrenia symptoms (16-channel resting-state EEG, 128 Hz sampling rate)
size_of_benchmark: 84 subjects (4,650 retained epochs after artifact rejection); 352 scattering coefficients per epoch across 16 channels
what_assessed_skills: EEG-based schizophrenia classification; biomarker discovery via multi-scale amplitude modulation and cross-frequency coupling features; spatial interpretability of discriminative EEG features
tasks_assessed: Binary classification (schizophrenia vs. healthy control) from resting-state EEG; biomarker identification using subject-level ANOVA with FDR correction; SHAP-based feature attribution and explainability
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation; Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) cross-validation (84 folds) with subject-level majority voting; metrics: Accuracy, Balanced Accuracy, Sensitivity, Specificity, F1-score, AUC-ROC, Cohen's κ, MCC. No LLMs used — classifiers are Random Forest and SVM (RBF).
llms_evaluated: None — study uses traditional ML classifiers (Random Forest, SVM with RBF kernel), not LLMs
performance_scores: Random Forest: Accuracy=90.48% (CI: 83.33–96.43%), Balanced Accuracy=90.09%, Sensitivity=95.56%, Specificity=84.62%, F1=91.49%, AUC-ROC=0.9339, Cohen's κ=0.8072, MCC=0.8110. SVM (RBF): Accuracy=79.76%, Sensitivity=82.22%, Specificity=76.92%, F1=81.32%, AUC-ROC=0.8860.
short_summary: This paper proposes a Wavelet Scattering Transform (WST) framework for interpretable schizophrenia classification and biomarker discovery from resting-state EEG. It addresses limitations of prior work (epoch-level cross-validation, static spectral features) by using multi-order WST coefficients to capture amplitude modulation and cross-frequency coupling, evaluated under strict Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation. Two traditional ML classifiers (Random Forest and SVM) were trained and evaluated on a public Kaggle EEG dataset of 84 adolescent subjects (45 schizophrenia, 39 healthy). SHAP explainability was applied to identify and validate key biomarkers. The Random Forest achieved 90.48% subject-level accuracy (AUC=0.9339, sensitivity=95.56%), with second-order gamma-band scattering coefficients at electrode P3 emerging as the most discriminative features. No LLMs were involved; this is a signal-processing/traditional-ML study on a psychiatric EEG dataset.

benchmark_name: WPG-MoE: Weak-Prior-Guided Dense Mixture-of-Experts for User-Level Social Media Depression Detection
authors: Xian Li; Yuanhe Tian; Yang Yang; Guoqing Wang; Yan Song
institutions: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Zhongguancun Academy; University of Science and Technology of China
ground_truth_source: SWDD: corrected self-report labels (manual audit of self_reported flag); Twitter depression dataset: self-reported user labels; eRisk25: official Task 2 labels. Human evidence-layout labels assigned by trained annotators (blinded, adjudicated) for 360 depressed + 1,800 control users across all three datasets.
size_of_benchmark: SWDD: 23,237 users (3,711 dep. / 19,526 ctrl.), ~4M posts; Twitter: 2,491 users (1,218 dep. / 1,273 ctrl.), ~896K posts; eRisk25: 909 users (102 dep. / 807 ctrl.), ~419K posts; Human-labeled diagnostic: 360 dep. + 1,800 ctrl. users; Post-level audit: 702 users / 5,820 posts
what_assessed_skills: User-level depression detection from social media post histories; handling heterogeneous evidence layouts (self-disclosure, episode-supported, sparse-evidence, mixed); PHQ-9-guided risk-post screening; mixture-of-experts routing guided by weak clinical priors; cross-dataset generalization
tasks_assessed: User-level binary depression classification from social media post histories; evidence-layout diagnostic (slice-level heterogeneity evaluation); cross-dataset transfer; ablation of routing components; controlled mixing experiments
population_represented: Social media users (Chinese Weibo/SWDD; English Twitter; English eRisk25); depressed and non-depressed individuals identified via self-report or clinical labels
evaluation_method: Automated evaluation on held-out test sets (80/10/10 stratified split); metrics: Recall, F1, AUROC, AUPRC (5-run mean); human evaluation for evidence-layout annotation (blinded A/B annotation + adjudication by C, Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α, raw agreement); Both (Automated + Human)
llms_evaluated: mDeBERTa-v3-base; BERT-base; Qwen3.5-0.8B; Qwen3.5-2B (default backbone); Ministral-3B; Ministral-8B. Offline privileged scorer: Qwen3-max API (training-only, not deployable backbone).
performance_scores: WPG-MoE (Qwen3.5-2B, SWDD in-domain): Rec=0.8050, F1=0.7490, AUROC=0.9490, AUPRC=0.8300; Twitter in-domain: Rec=0.8440, F1=0.7630, AUROC=0.9290, AUPRC=0.8520; eRisk25 in-domain: Rec=0.8210, F1=0.7440, AUROC=0.9260, AUPRC=0.7350. Gains over matched Base (Qwen3.5-2B): +0.07 F1, +0.08 AUROC, +0.08 AUPRC across datasets.
short_summary: This paper proposes WPG-MoE, a weak-prior-guided dense Mixture-of-Experts framework for user-level depression detection from social media, addressing post-screening evidence heterogeneity. The core insight is that depressed users express risk through heterogeneous evidence layouts (self-disclosure, episode-supported, sparse-evidence, mixed), which a monolithic classifier fails to handle well. WPG-MoE uses PHQ-9-guided screening at inference and LLM-derived structured evidence (Qwen3-max) as training-only privileged routing priors under a Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) framework, with five specialized dense experts over a shared LLM backbone. The system is evaluated on three datasets (SWDD/Chinese, Twitter/English, eRisk25/English) using automated metrics (Recall, F1, AUROC, AUPRC) and human evidence-layout annotation (κ=0.707), with both in-domain and cross-dataset transfer protocols. WPG-MoE consistently outperforms seven strong baselines and multiple backbone variants, with the largest gains for sparse-evidence and episode-supported users.
